result:
The Department of Unfinished Things occupied the fourth floor of a building that had only three.

To reach it, you had to enter the lift while thinking about something you meant to do. The birthday card still in your desk. The language you were going to learn. The shelf.

Especially the shelf.

The lift knew a great deal about shelves.

When Mara arrived, a clerk was untangling a necklace beside a sign that read:

**PLEASE HAVE YOUR EXCUSES READY.**

“I didn’t know this place existed,” she said.

“That’s the most common one.” He pushed a form toward her. “What have you brought?”

“Nothing.”

The clerk glanced at her hands.

She was holding a blue notebook.

“Oh,” she said.

Inside were thirty-seven pages of a novel she had begun at twenty-three. She was forty-one now. In the intervening years she had moved six times, married once, learned to make bread, and developed firm opinions about dishwasher loading. The notebook had accompanied her through all of it, occupying increasingly inaccessible drawers.

“I suppose you’re going to tell me to finish it.”

“Good heavens, no,” said the clerk. “We’re understaffed as it is.”

He led her into the archive.

There were half-knitted jumpers sleeping on shelves. An enormous glasshouse contained gardens nobody had planted. Somewhere, an orchestra repeatedly played the first eight bars of something promising.

In one corner stood a door.

“What’s through there?” Mara asked.

“A conversation someone keeps rehearsing.”

“Does it ever happen?”

“Sometimes. Then we can use the room for storage.”

They stopped at a desk overlooking a courtyard. On the desk sat a kettle, two cups, and a wastepaper basket.

“You have three options,” the clerk said. “Continue it. Let it go. Or leave it here awhile.”

“What’s the difference between leaving it here and keeping it in a drawer?”

“The drawer charges interest.”

Mara opened the notebook.

The first sentence was terrible.

She laughed.

The second sentence was also terrible, but with ambition.

By page four she had found a description of rain that she liked. By page nine she remembered the room where she had written it: the sloping ceiling, the cold tea, the neighbour practising trumpet badly and without shame.

“I don’t think I want to write this book anymore,” she said.

The clerk poured the tea.

For a while she read, occasionally wincing. Then she tore out a blank page from the back.

“May I have a pen?”

The clerk checked his pockets, opened two drawers, and finally extracted one from behind his ear.

At the top of the page she wrote:

*Things I would enjoy doing now.*

“Does that count as starting something?” she asked.

“I’m afraid so.”

“Will I have to come back?”

“Probably.”

She put the notebook in the basket, then took it out again.

“The rain,” she explained.

The clerk handed her a pair of scissors.
